newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ballast Nedam sees '97 net up five pct.
newsitem.headline: Ballast Nedam sees '97 net up five pct.

text.p: Construction group Ballast Nedam NV said on Thursday it expected profit growth in 1997 of at least five percent.
"Because we do not see any increase in share capital at this moment, this will result in a similar rise of profits per share," the company said in a statement.

Ballast Nedam, which is 48 percent owned by Germany's Hochtief AG, earlier posted a 1996 net profit of 91.5 million guilders, down from 1995's 92.1 million. Ballast Nedam had previously predicted a 1996 profit near the 1995 level.
The company's turnover rose to 3.82 billion guilders from 1995's 3.01 billion. It is expected that turnover levels can be maintained at this higher level in 1997, Ballast Nedam said.

It said that about half of the turnover growth in 1996 was caused by the takover of British builder Wiltshier Plc by the end of 1995 but added that this firm had not yet contributed to Ballast Nedam's profits.

By the end of last year, the group's order book totalled 3.6 billion guilders, compared with 2.7 billion a year earlier. The size and composition of the order portfolio give good starting positions in 1997, the company said.
Ballast Nedam said its marginally lower total year net profit implied that it had compensated the major part of the setback of the first half of the year.
In July, it reported 1996 first-half net profits had fallen by 18 percent to 32 million guilders.
The company said it had generated most of its turnover growth in the Netherlands, where price competition remained sharp, and in Britain.
Turnover growth had slowed at the beginning of the year because of the harsh winter. This was offset later in the year but at extra costs.
Capacity utilisation of the dredging fleet improved in the second half of 1996 and because more projects were offered in the market, price levels also recovered in this sector.

Ballast Nedam said it aimed at improving margins in all its units by increasing efficiency and productivity, so that all subsidiaries could compare themselves with the best performing players in each sector.

Because turnover is shifting towards western Europe, where most of the orders are finished in the second half of the year, there will be a larger difference between first and second half results, it said.
